source_facts.claim: The Computational Democracy Project continues to describe Polis as an open-source, real-time system for gathering, analyzing, and understanding what large groups think in their own words using statistics and machine learning.

The current Polis documentation says participants submit short statements and respond to other statements with agree, disagree, or pass, while participants themselves create the dimensions of the inquiry.
The maintained public repository describes Polis as an AI-powered sentiment-gathering platform and identifies its public deployment and knowledge base.
Field Note 25 imagines collective storms that may not end in consensus and may instead produce public artifacts preserving sources, disagreement, alternatives, ratification, and unresolved questions.
source_facts.locator: The storm does not necessarily end in consensus.; It may settle into a durable public artifact:

cartographer.inference: The existing Polis proposals remain a useful adjacency for large-group sensemaking. Polis maps participant statements and response patterns, while Field Note 25 imagines a wider public object carrying testimony, evidence, art, values, provenance, alternatives, and unresolved disagreement.
cartographer.uncertainty: The relationship remains model-proposed. This comparison does not imply endorsement, partnership, methodological equivalence, or that an opinion map captures every form of difference.
cartographer.attribution: External facts come from the official Computational Democracy Project site, Polis documentation, and maintained public repository. Internal facts come from the exact public Field Notes source.
cartographer.no_proposal_reason: The bounded source recheck continued to support the existing node and edge proposals. A new candidate would duplicate the current proposal queue.
